claims.text: High configurational entropy and local lattice distortion jointly govern the thermal stability of HEA nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy and local lattice distortion suppress atomic diffusion at lower temperatures.
Suppressed diffusion allows a single-phase solid solution to be retained up to a critical temperature.
Above the critical temperature, diffusion accelerates and causes elemental segregation.
Elemental segregation preferentially initiates at grain boundaries and particle surfaces.
Atomic mobility is higher at grain boundaries and surface regions than in the grain interiors.
Increasing temperature allows the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation to overcome kinetic barriers.
Selective elemental migration then nucleates secondary phases at grain boundaries and surfaces.
Thermal activation induces Cr-V segregation in tungsten-based HEAs.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions with nanocrystalline grains and uniform elemental distributions.
Below the critical temperature, the nanoparticles will retain a uniform single-phase solid solution with minimal segregation.
Above the critical temperature, secondary precipitates or segregated phases will appear at grain boundaries and surfaces.
Secondary-phase formation will produce compositional gradients and distinct XRD peaks.
An inert atmosphere minimizes extrinsic chemical effects so observed changes primarily reflect thermal diffusion and intrinsic phase separation.
Sufficient holding time at each temperature can bring the nanoparticles near equilibrium.
The segregation threshold and identity of segregated phases depend on alloy system, particle size, and surface energy.
Exceptionally strong elemental affinity or repulsion and particle-size effects can cause deviations from the predicted behavior.
The nanoparticles will be heated incrementally from 473 K to 1923 K and compared with the as-synthesized baseline using XRD, TEM, and APT.
